abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Patients undergoing chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR T)‐cell therapy are at risk of developing immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). We observed an upregulation of CCR5 and CCR2 expression in CD4+ T cells among patients who developed ICANS. Notably, increased CCR5 expression was detectable as early as day one post‐infusion, but only in those who eventually developed ICANS, suggesting a potential role for CCR5 as an early biomarker for ICANS onset.

sec.p: Keywords: CAR‐T cells, chemokines, ICANS, lymphomas, macrophages
Received 2025 Jan 22; Accepted 2025 Jun 12; Issue date 2025 Sep.

Adoptive cellular therapy has revolutionized cancer treatment, offering curative potential for patients with B‐cell lymphomas. Anti‐CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR‐T)‐cell therapies have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in relapsed/refractory diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (DLBCL), achieving regulatory approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA). 1 , 2 CAR‐T therapy involves engineering a patient's T cells to target CD19, a protein expressed on B cells, leading to impressive response rates and durable remissions.

Despite its success, CAR‐T therapy is associated with significant immune‐related toxicities, primarily cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). 3 ICANS, a neurotoxicity unique to CAR‐T therapy, manifests as cognitive changes, motor deficits, seizures or, in severe cases, cerebral oedema, affecting 21%–64% of patients and occurring severely in 10%–28%. 1 , 2

The mechanisms of ICANS involve endothelial dysfunction linked to CRS. Cytokines released during CRS activate endothelial cells, causing vascular leakage and blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption. This allows immune cells and cytokines to infiltrate the central nervous system (CNS), triggering neuroinflammation. Emerging evidence suggests CAR‐T cells targeting CD19 may directly impair BBB integrity by interacting with CD19 antigens on pericytes. 4 Cytokines such as GM‐CSF, IL‐6 and IL‐1 are implicated in ICANS pathophysiology, and interventions like the IL‐1 receptor antagonist anakinra have shown promise in severe cases. 5

CCR5, a receptor involved in immune cell trafficking, 6 has been implicated in the mechanism of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in the context of progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy (PML). Targeting CCR5 with therapies like maraviroc has reduced CNS immune infiltration in PML‐related IRIS condition. 7 Similarly, CCR2 facilitates monocyte chemotaxis during inflammation. This study explores their roles in ICANS development, providing insights into mechanisms and potential interventions to mitigate CAR‐T‐associated neurotoxicity.

This prospective study was conducted at Rambam Health Care Campus in collaboration with the Bone Marrow Transplant Unit and Neuroimmunology Laboratory. Institutional review board approval was obtained (protocol 0333‐22‐RMB), and written informed consent was secured from all participants. Patients aged ≥18 years with relapsed/refractory DLBCL treated with CD19‐directed CAR‐T cells (axi‐cel or tisa‐cel) were eligible for enrolment. Baseline Positron Emission Tomography‐Computed Tomography (PET‐CT) scans were performed prior to lymphodepletion, and disease burden was assessed using Lugano criteria. 8

Before CAR‐T‐cell infusion, patients received lymphodepleting chemotherapy consisting of cyclophosphamide (250–500 mg/m2) and fludarabine (25–30 mg/m2) for 3 days or bendamustine (90 mg/m2 for 2 days). CAR‐T cells were thawed and infused per manufacturer guidelines. Patients received prophylactic anticonvulsants (Keppra) to mitigate ICANS risk, and corticosteroids were administered to treat ICANS when clinically indicated. Toxicities, including CRS and ICANS, were graded according to the ASTCT consensus criteria, as well as immune effector cell‐associated haematotoxicity (ICAHT) and immune effector cell‐associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis‐like syndrome (IEC‐HS) criteria. 9 , 10 , 11 The diagnosis of ICANS was made after careful consideration of differential diagnoses, including infections (e.g. viral or bacterial encephalitis), medication‐related effects (e.g. opioids, anticonvulsants), cerebrovascular accidents or intracranial bleeding, metabolic disturbances and central nervous system involvement by lymphoma.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were collected at baseline (before lymphodepletion) and on days 1 and 3 post‐infusion. An additional sample was collected from each patient between days 3 and 8, as these are the time points when ICANS typically emerges. PBMCs were isolated using gradient centrifugation and stained for flow cytometry analysis. The gating strategy is illustrated in Figure S1. Markers of interest included chemokine receptors CCR5 and CCR2 (on CD3+/CD4+ cells) and macrophage polarization markers such as CD80, CD23, CD163, CD83 and CD206 (on CD14+ cells). Table S1 provides details on the fluorochromes, antibody clones, instrument models and reference controls utilized in this study.

Statistical analysis and graphs were performed using Prism version 10.2.1 software (GraphPad, San Diego CA, USA). To compare differences between the ICANS and non‐ICANS groups, we used multiple t‐tests (parametric), followed by the two‐stage linear step‐up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli for multiple testing correction. For the prediction analysis, we applied a two‐way ANOVA to identify differences in both row and column factors. Additionally, we used multiple t‐tests (parametric), along with the two‐stage linear step‐up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli, to evaluate differences between baseline and day 1, as well as between baseline and day 3. A p‐value of p ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Additional statistical methods are supplied in Table S1.

Sixteen patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL were enrolled between August 2023 and October 2024. The median age was 66.5 years (range: 46–81), and the cohort included 62% male and 38% female participants. Most patients (63%) had de novo DLBCL, while three patients had CNS involvement at the time of CAR‐T‐cell infusion. All patients received axi‐cel or tisa‐cel CAR‐T‐cell products, and toxicities were carefully monitored and managed (Table S2).

All patients experienced CRS of any grade, with three experiencing high‐grade CRS. ICANS developed in nine patients (56%), ranging from grade 1 to grade 4. Eight of these patients required steroid treatment, and all cases resolved following appropriate intervention (Table S3).

Chemokine receptor expressions were evaluated in CD3+/CD4+ T cells. A representative patient who developed ICANS is demonstrated in Figure 1A. Patients who developed ICANS exhibited a significant increase in CCR5 expression, rising from 55.4% (range: 42.5%–71.3%) at baseline to 89.5% (range: 77.9%–94.4%) by days 3–8 post‐infusion (p = 0.001) (Figure 1B). Non‐ICANS patients, by contrast, demonstrated a decrease in CCR5 levels, from 61.9% (range: 33.1%–83.3%) to 44.7% (range: 25.4%–81.1%). Similarly, CCR2 levels increased significantly in ICANS patients, from 35.1% (range: 29.3%–48.9%) to 65.8% (range: 51.8%–81.7%; p = 0.0037), while non‐ICANS patients showed only minor decreases (Figure 1C).

We analysed CCR5 and CCR2 expression on CD3posCD4pos cells before and after CAR‐T infusion, comparing the ICANS and non‐ICANS groups. (A) Schematic timeline of representative patient that developed ICANS. (B) CCR5 expression on CD3posCD4pos cells. (C) CCR2 expression on CD3posCD4pos cells. [Colour figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com]

sec.p: In higher grade ICANS cases, CCR5 levels were proportionally higher compared to lower grade cases, but this was not statistically significant (Figure S2). Notably, no significant differences were observed for CCR7 and CCR6 expressions between ICANS and non‐ICANS groups (Figure S3).

As certain variables are known to be associated with an increased risk of ICANS, we next stratified CCR5 changes according to these factors. The results are presented in Table S4. There were no significant differences between patients with an increase in CCR5 and those with no change in CCR5 with respect to age, CRS severity or tocilizumab administration. However, patients who had progressive disease at the time of lymphodepletion were more likely to exhibit an increase in CCR5.

Markers of macrophage polarization, including pro‐inflammatory CD80 and anti‐inflammatory CD23, CD163, CD83 and CD206, were analysed in CD14+ monocytes. No significant differences in macrophage polarization profiles were observed between ICANS and non‐ICANS groups (Figure S4).

CCR5 expression was significantly elevated in ICANS patients as early as day 1 post‐infusion, rising from 46.5% (range: 14.2%–71.3%) to 78.3% (range: 62.2–96.5%; p = 0.031). By day 3, CCR5 levels reached 93.1% (range: 91.1%–98.0%; p = 0.00064) in ICANS patients, whereas non‐ICANS patients showed no significant increases (Figure 2A). CCR2, while elevated in ICANS patients, did not demonstrate predictive value (Figure 2B). These findings suggest that CCR5 upregulation may serve as an early biomarker for ICANS risk. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated that CCR5 expression at day 3 effectively discriminates between patients with and without ICANS, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9841(Figure S5).

caption.p: Upregulation of CCR5 and CCR2 prior to clinical ICANS. We analysed CCR5 and CCR2 expression on CD3posCD4pos cells before and 1 and 3 days post‐CAR‐T infusion, comparing the ICANS and non‐ICANS groups. (A) CCR5 expression on CD3posCD4pos cells. (B) CCR2 expression on CD3posCD4pos cells.

sec.p: CAR‐T‐cell therapy has revolutionized treatment for relapsed/refractory DLBCL, offering durable remissions where traditional therapies fail. 1 However, its use is limited by severe toxicities like CRS and ICANS. 3 While CRS is better understood and often managed with cytokine blockers (e.g. tocilizumab), ICANS remains complex and poorly defined. This study provides key insights into ICANS pathophysiology, highlighting opportunities for improved risk stratification and treatment.

This study identifies CCR5 as a possible key mediator of ICANS, with its expression on CD3+/CD4+ cells significantly upregulated in ICANS patients as early as day 1 post‐infusion. By day 3, CCR5 levels were further elevated, particularly in severe cases, underscoring its potential as a predictive biomarker and driver of ICANS severity. These findings align with prior studies linking CCR5 to BBB dysfunction and neuroinflammation in conditions like multiple sclerosis (MS) and PML. 7 Notably, in MS patients, CCR5 expression on monocytes was downregulated following alemtuzumab therapy, a lymphocyte‐depleting agent. 12

Herich et al. identified a subpopulation of CD4+ T effector memory cells, with high expression of CCR5 and functionally recruiting granzyme K to migrate through the BBB under homeostatic conditions and subsequently be found in the CNS. 13

Additionally, preclinical data show that severe peripheral inflammation may increase CCL5/CCR5 axis activation in multiple inflammatory cell types, such as microglia, astrocytes and monocytes, resulting in BBB disruption and neurobehavioural dysfunction. 14 Importantly, bone marrow (BM)‐directed gene delivery of RNAi targeting CCR5 effectively downregulates CCR5 expression in BM‐derived cells, reducing their trafficking into the CNS and providing significant neuroprotection against excitotoxic injury. 15 These findings along with ours highlight the role of CCR5 and its ligands, in promoting CNS inflammation and injury by facilitating PBMC infiltration across the cerebrovascular endothelium.

In contrast to CCR5, CCR2 showed only modest changes in expression and did not demonstrate significant predictive value for ICANS. While CCR2 has been implicated in monocyte recruitment during inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, 16 it is possible that CCR2 acts downstream of CCR5 or contributes to neuroinflammation through indirect mechanisms. These findings, if supported by larger clinical trials, suggest that future research should assess targeting CCR5 over CCR2 for the prevention and treatment of ICANS.
We observed no significant differences in macrophage polarization markers between ICANS and non‐ICANS patients, suggesting macrophage activity in peripheral blood is not a key driver of ICANS.

Several mechanisms have been proposed for the development of ICANS. The primary hypothesis points to systemic inflammation and cytokine production. 17 Additionally, endothelial activation 18 and disruption of BBB function 18 have been implied in ICANS pathophysiology. Interleukin‐1 and interleukin‐6 were also reported to be associated with severe ICANS. 19 However, the role of chemokines in ICANS development remains unexplored. ICANS mostly develops following CRS, which triggers endothelial activation and a subsequent decrease in tight junction expression. 20 This process has been closely associated with CCR5, which plays a significant role in endothelial barrier dysfunction, a process linked to CCR5. 14 The disruption of the BBB during CRS may be driven by the combined activity of both CCR5 and CCR2, which are involved in inflammatory pathways that affect endothelial cells. 4

Despite these promising findings, this study has several limitations. The small sample size and single‐centre design may limit the generalizability of the results. Additionally, while this study focused on patients treated with axi‐cel and tisa‐cel, other CAR‐T‐cell products may elicit distinct immunologic responses that could affect CCR5 expression.

This study highlights CCR5's pivotal role in ICANS pathophysiology, with its upregulation detectable prior to symptom onset, allowing for risk stratification and pre‐emptive interventions. CCR5 shows promise as a predictive biomarker and therapeutic target, offering potential strategies to mitigate ICANS, after ensuring CAR‐T efficacy despite this treatment.

The findings are preliminary and warrant external validation. Further studies in larger, multicentre cohorts are necessary to confirm these outcomes. Future studies should include correlative analyses of CCR5 expression on CAR‐T cells and in CSF to evaluate CCR5‐targeted interventions across diverse patient populations.
